Article Title: Government proposes stricter anti-paper leak law, faster investigation and trials
Article Text:
Government proposes stricter anti-paper leak laws to safeguard against leaks

NEW DELHI: Tightening the noose around individuals, service providers and organised gangs involved in paper leaks, the Centre has proposed longer jail terms, steeper fines, and time-bound investigation and disposal of trials and appeals.According to the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill circulated to Members of Parliament, the minimum jail term for offences committed by individuals, as well as directors, senior management personnel or persons in charge of service providers conducting public examinations, has been increased to five years. In cases involving organised crime, the minimum imprisonment has been proposed at seven years.The Bill proposes that any person resorting to unfair means or committing offences under the law shall be punished with imprisonment of at least five years, which may extend to 10 years, along with a fine of up to Rs 50 lakh.It also proposes that any service provider found guilty would face a fine of up to Rs 5 crore — a five-fold increase over the existing provision — and would be barred from conducting public examinations for eight years, compared with the current four-year debarment.If an investigation establishes that an offence was committed with the consent or connivance of any director, senior management personnel or person in charge of a service provider, such individuals would be liable to a minimum imprisonment of five years, extendable up to 10 years. The proposed maximum fine has also been increased from the existing Rs 1 crore to Rs 5 crore.Seeking to amend Section 11 of the 2024 Act dealing with organised crime, the Bill proposes that if a person or group of persons, including an examination authority, service provider or any other institution, commits an organised crime, the minimum jail term would be increased to eight years from the current five years. The maximum penalty would also be raised tenfold to Rs 10 crore.To ensure speedy investigations, the Bill proposes that the government may constitute a Central Investigation Agency or a Special Task Force (STF). Where an STF has been constituted, it would carry out the investigation. The Bill also seeks to insert a new provision mandating that every investigation be completed within two months.For faster trials, the Bill provides for day-to-day proceedings and empowers states to establish Special Fast Track Courts in consultation with the Chief Justice of the respective High Court. It mandates that trial proceedings shall continue on a day-to-day basis until all witnesses in attendance have been examined.The Special Fast Track Courts would be required to dispose of cases within three months from the date of filing of the chargesheet.The Bill further proposes that any appeal against an order of a Special Fast Track Court shall be heard by a division bench of the High Court, which must dispose of the appeal within three months. It also mandates that every appeal be filed within 30 days from the date of the order.
Article Summary: Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill circulated to Members of Parliament. Minimum jail term for offences committed by individuals, as well as directors, senior management personnel or persons in charge of service providers conducting public examinations, has been increased to five years. In cases involving organised crime, the minimum imprisonment has been proposed at seven years.

Article Title: Deepwater drilling begins in Mahanadi basin to assess hydrocarbon reserves
Article Text:
India's next energy frontier is deep waters: Hardeep Puri as ONGC begins Mahanadi drilling

NEW DELHI: State-owned Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) spudded the first deepwater appraisal well in the Mahanadi offshore basin Friday, marking a key step in assessing the hydrocarbon potential of one of India’s most prospective offshore regions and paving the way for higher domestic oil and gas production.The well, named MN-DWN18-1-HD, is the first of four planned deepwater appraisal wells in the basin. The drilling programme, under govt’s Samudra Manthan mission, will use deepwater technology to evaluate the commercial viability of hydrocarbon reserves.Building on the recent Utkal and Konark discoveries that have strengthened the hydrocarbon prospectivity of the Mahanadi offshore basin, ONGC said the well is being drilled around 23 nautical miles from the Konark discovery off the Odisha coast.Petroleum minister Hardeep Singh Puri, who flagged off the drilling virtually, said the exercise marks “the beginning of a new chapter” in India’s efforts to strengthen energy security and reduce dependence on imported crude oil and natural gas.India imports nearly 90% of its crude oil requirement and about half of its natural gas demand, making higher domestic production a key component of its long-term energy security strategy to reduce exposure to global supply disruptions and price volatility.The appraisal drilling is expected to provide a clearer assessment of the basin’s resource potential before any commercial development is taken up.The minister said a series of policy reforms over the past decade have reshaped the country’s exploration and production sector. These include the Hydrocarbon Exploration and Licensing Policy (HELP), the Open Acreage Licensing Programme (OALP), a revenue-sharing regime, and opening nearly 99% of the country’s previously restricted offshore “No-Go” areas for exploration.According to the minister, about 81% of India’s active exploration acreage has been awarded since 2014, reflecting increased investor interest following the reforms.Puri said govt has also expanded geoscientific data generation through initiatives such as Mission Anveshan, the National Seismic Programme and the National Data Repository to improve exploration success in frontier basins.Under OALP, 172 exploration blocks covering nearly 3.8 lakh sq km have been awarded so far, attracting committed investments of more than $4.3 billion. During 2025-26, around 674 exploration wells were drilled, five new hydrocarbon discoveries were made, and seven discoveries were brought into production, he said.The minister said govt’s strategy is focused on both discovering new oil and gas resources and improving recovery from existing producing fields by deploying advanced technologies and global best practices.
Article Summary: State-owned Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) spudded the first deepwater appraisal well in the Mahanadi offshore basin Friday. The drilling programme, under govt’s Samudra Manthan mission, will use deepwater technology to evaluate the commercial viability of hydrocarbon reserves.

Article Title: 'To ensure anti-national elements don't benefit from situation': Dharmendra Pradhan resigns - read full text of letter
Article Text:
Read his full statement

NEW DELHI: Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan on Saturday tendered his resignation from the council of ministers amid the ongoing protests over the NEET paper leak.In a letter addressed to his "young friends," Pradhan said that he has sent his resignation to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, considering the situation that has developed at Jantar Mantar and across the country.He said he sent his resignation letter to PM Modi so that "anti-national forces do not take advantage of this situation". Pradhan added that the "unity of the country should be preserved ... not even a single student's future should get entangled in legal complications, and our children should devote their time to studies and focus on building their careers".My Young Friends,I have been dedicated to students, teachers, and education reform for more than four decades. I have always believed that a strong, inclusive, and visionary education system is the very foundation of a strong nation.I deeply respect the aspirations, emotions, and just expectations of the country's youth. Realizing the dreams of India's young generation has been a moral commitment of all of us in political and social life. I express my gratitude to the Hon'ble Prime Minister for the opportunity he gave me to serve the nation under his visionary leadership.However, irregularities came to light in the NEET-UG examination held on 3 May 2026. The Government of India took immediate cognizance of this, handed over the investigation to the CBI, cancelled the examination, and announced a new date for the re-examination. Alongside this, it was decided that from next year the examination would be conducted in CBT (Computer-Based Test) mode.During this period, our foremost priority was to ensure that the examination for more than 20 lakh (2 million) students was conducted smoothly. This was carried out under a "whole of government" approach. In this, along with the Government of India, the state governments — especially the district administrations — played an important role. With the cooperation of students and parents, this examination was completed on 21 June 2026.From the very first day, I took responsibility and never turned away from this situation. My resolve was that we would not let any meritorious student's chances be ruined because of an examination mafia, and that no injustice would be done to any student.The NEET-UG results declared on 16 July were satisfactory, with many meritorious students from poor backgrounds also achieving success.However, during this time too, certain individuals occupying positions of responsibility tried to mislead students and create obstruction, which caused me deep anguish.I have always been an unwavering believer in the strength of our democracy, and I have always held deep respect for the aspirations, dreams, and expectations of the youth. They are not only India's future, but also the bearers, builders, and architects of a new and developed India.Watching the events of the last 10 days has saddened me. This is not a matter of personal reputation for me.The youth power of India is the real strength of this country.My resolve is that we will not let the country's youth get caught in a web of confusion.Considering the situation that has developed at Jantar Mantar and across the country — that anti-national forces should not take advantage of this situation, that the unity of the country should be preserved, that not even a single student's future should get entangled in legal complications, and that our children should devote their time to studies and focus on building their careers — I have sent my resignation to the Hon'ble Prime Minister.I express my heartfelt gratitude to the Hon'ble Prime Minister for his guidance, trust, and continuous support. I also express my gratitude to all my esteemed colleagues in the Council of Ministers, the officials and staff of the Ministry, and all those with whom I had the privilege of working. Service to the nation is the highest priority of my life, and I shall remain dedicated to it always.By the blessings of Lord Sri Jagannath, I shall continue to dedicate myself in every possible way, in the future as well, to the fulfillment of the aspirations of Mother India, the people of Odisha, and the youth of the country."
Article Summary: Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan tendered his resignation from the council of ministers. He said he sent his resignation letter to PM Modi so that "anti-national forces do not take advantage of this situation" He said the "unity of the country should be preserved... not even a single student's future should get entangled in legal complications"

Article Title: What is the Public Examinations Amendment Bill? Govt proposes sweeping changes to anti-cheating law
Article Text:
Investigations into offences under the Act will have to be completed within two months.

Stricter penalities introduced

NEW DELHI: The Centre has proposed sweeping changes to the anti-cheating law, seeking to speed up investigations and time-bound trials while introducing tougher punishment for those involved in paper leaks and examination malpractice.Under the proposed Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, the central government to constitute a special task force (STF), wherever necessary, for investigation of offences under the Act.Thereupon, investigations into offences under the Act will have to be completed within two months.After that, within three months from the date of filing of the chargesheet, a time-bound appeal mechanism in the amendment requires the special fast track courts to conduct trials on a day-to-day basis and complete it.Appeals against judgments, sentences or orders passed by a special fast track court will lie before a two-judge bench of the high court, which will be required to dispose of such appeals within three months of their admission.To facilitate this, the Bill empowers all state governments and Union Territory administrations to designate any Court of Session as a special fast track court for trying offences under the Act.According to the Statement of Objects and Reasons, the amendment aims to strengthen the credibility of public examinations by ensuring speedy investigation, time-bound trials and stronger deterrence against paper leaks and organised examination malpractice.For individuals found guilty of offences under the Act, the proposed punishment has been enhanced. The minimum imprisonment has been increased from three years to five years, while the maximum jail term has been raised from five years to 10 years. The maximum fine has also been increased from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 50 lakh.The Bill also proposes stricter action against service providers involved in examination fraud. The maximum fine for such entities has been increased from Rs 1 crore to Rs 5 crore, while the period during which they can be barred from conducting public examinations has been doubled from four years to eight years.Directors, senior managers or other persons responsible for the conduct of the business of a service provider, if found to have connived in the offence, will face a minimum imprisonment of five years, compared with the existing minimum of three years. The proposed fine for such persons has also been increased from Rs 1 crore to Rs 5 crore.The amendment further enhances punishment for organised crime related to paper leaks. The minimum jail term has been increased from five years to seven years, while the proposed maximum fine has been raised from Rs 1 crore to Rs 10 crore.
Article Summary: Under the proposed Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, investigations into offences under the Act will have to be completed within two months. A time-bound appeal mechanism in the amendment requires the special fast track courts to conduct trials on a day-to-day basis.

Article Title: 2 new secretaries in education ministry, Vineet Joshi moved to panchayati raj
Article Text:
Joshi moved to panchayati raj

NEW DELHI: Amid ongoing protests over NEET-UG paper leak issue, govt Thursday named new secretaries for higher and school education departments, with incumbent Vineet Joshi, who had charge of both, moved to low-profile panchayati raj department.While animal husbandry secretary Naresh Pal Gangwar was appointed the new secretary for higher education, TK Anil Kumar will be the new school education secretary. The changes mark an overhaul of sorts in education ministry bureaucracy, as Abhishek Singh was earlier named head of the National Testing Agency , which conducts NEET, CUET and other exams.In early June, CBSE chief Rahul Singh and secretary Himanshu Gupta were transferred out of the National Testing Agency after a controversy over on-screen marking.The secretary-level appointments included 13 new department heads, including a bifurcation of ministry of housing and urban affairs. MoHUA secretary K Srinivas has been shifted to development of north eastern region (DoNER) ministry. D Thara, from Gujarat cadre, has been appointed secretary of the just-created department of capital development, while her batchmate Satendra Singh from Jharkhand will lead the department of urban development.The changes in education ministry are significant as govt has said demand for removal of education minister Dharmendra Pradhan is not under consideration, but steps will be taken to address concerns. The appointments committee of cabinet also desginated Chandra Bhushan Kumar as new labour secretary, while Keshav Chandra will be the new mines secretary. Odisha cadre IAS officer SK Lohani has been designated as animal husbandry secretary.
Article Summary: Vineet Joshi, who had charge of both, moved to low-profile panchayati raj department. The changes mark an overhaul of sorts in education ministry bureaucracy. Abhishek Singh was earlier named head of the National Testing Agency.

Article Title: 'Paper leaks are no ordinary matter': What PM Modi said in his midnight video message
Article Text:
PM Modi promises tougher action in midnight address

Poll Vote & Share your view What will help restore trust in public exams the most? Fast action against offenders Stronger exam systems 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: With CJP-led protests over NEET-UG 2026 examination irregularities showing no signs of easing, Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday said the government would take stricter action against paper leaks."Friends, I know that paper leaks are not an ordinary matter. For lakhs of students and their parents, it is extremely painful," PM Modi said in a self-recorded video posted on X.PM Modi said the Union Cabinet would consider a draft Bill proposing Fast-Track Courts and stringent punishment for offenders."In the last two and a half months since the paper leak incidents, several major steps have been taken. The culprits have been caught; they are currently in jail," he added.PM Modi highlighted that the government made every effort to ensure that the students did not lose an academic year."Our most important responsibility was to ensure that a whole year for the students is not wasted. It was very important to conduct the exams immediately. The government used its full strength to arrange exams for nearly 22 lakh students in the shortest possible time. And just five or six days ago, on the 19th, the results were also announced.News of the happiness of successful students is coming from all over the country. "PM Modi said that the government has decided to take stronger measures to tackle paper leaks."However, we are not among those who are satisfied with just that. And therefore, today I have issued directions to the departments to set up Fast-Track Courts. The departments worked tirelessly and, late last night, provided me with a draft. This draft, which includes provisions for Fast-Track Courts and stringent punishments, will be discussed in the Cabinet tomorrow," he added."After incorporating suggestions from Cabinet colleagues, it will be given a final shape. Efforts will be made to get this Bill passed in the House as soon as possible, as the second week of the Parliament session begins on Monday," he said.The PM also urged activist Sonam Wangchuk to follow doctors' advice, recover well and gain weight as soon as possible."I urge Sonam ji to follow his routine as per the doctors' advice and regain his old weight as soon as possible. I pray to the Lord that Sonam ji remains healthy," he said in a post on X.Activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike on Friday at Medanta Hospital in the presence of Union ministers J P Nadda and Jitendra Singh, along with senior leaders of the Apex Body of Leh Ladakh.In a post on X, Wangchuk said he decided to call off the fast after prolonged negotiations on various conditions and in view of the possibility of violence in the country.The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which has been spearheading the protest at Jantar Mantar, welcomed Wangchuk's decision but said its agitation would continue until Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.
Article Summary: PM Modi said the Union Cabinet would consider a draft Bill proposing Fast-Track Courts and stringent punishment for offenders. Activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike on Friday. The Cockroach Janta Party welcomed Wangchuk's decision but said its agitation would continue until Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.

Article Title: IndiGo opposes more say for airport operators in airlines
Article Text:
Rahul Bhatia, promoter and MD of India’s largest carrier IndiGo

NEW DELHI: Rahul Bhatia, promoter and MD of India's largest carrier IndiGo , has opposed the proposed move to allow airport operators in India to own and run airlines too. "There is no global precedent for this. It raises massive conflict-of-interest concerns, and it is unclear how such a move would serve consumers' interests," he said at a post earnings call.Bhatia's Thursday comments come as govt is considering to dilute provisions that disallow operators of Delhi and Mumbai airports to own more than 10% stake in a scheduled airline. While the Adani Group, which runs Mumbai airport, is likely to make the first move by picking up stake in an existing airline or investing in a startup, the GMR Group, which operates Delhi's IGIA, could do so at a subsequent stage.The news has resulted in Interglobe Aviation's shares falling for two consecutive days as investors perceive the airline, which controls two-thirds of the domestic aviation market, to be a loser in case the move goes through.Senior aviation ministry officials said a country with the economic potential of India should have multiple airlines and not just a duopoly with IndiGo and Tata's Air India group.Meanwhile, the Competition Commission of India (CCI) Thursday invited public comments on a commitment proposal by IndiGo in a probe following its last Dec schedule collapse.The airline has proposed temporarily releasing domestic slots at airports. "Post such handover, the airport operator/authority may determine re-allocation of such slots/dates for routes, as deemed fit," the CCI notice says.
Article Summary: Rahul Bhatia, promoter and MD of India's largest carrier IndiGo, has opposed the proposed move to allow airport operators in India to own and run airlines too. "There is no global precedent for this. It raises massive conflict-of-interest concerns, and it is unclear how such a move would serve consumers' interests," he said.

Article Title: CJP, Centre set for 12:30 pm talks at Constitution Club; Pradhan's resignation among key demand
Article Text:
CJP-Centre meeting to be held today (ANI)

'Peaceful protest will continue'

NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) delegation will meet Union ministers at the Constitution Club of India at 12.30 pm on Friday, after the Centre agreed to hold talks at a neutral venue—a key demand raised by the outfit during its ongoing agitation over the NEET row.The meeting comes a day after activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike at Medanta Hospital in the presence of Union ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh, paving the way for formal discussions between the government and the protesters.Confirming the development, CJP chief spokesperson Saurav Das said the organisation welcomed the government's decision to shift the talks to a neutral venue."Our protest will continue; Constitution Club of India chosen as venue for meeting with government ministers, hoping for an open-minded dialogue," Das told reporters on Thursday.CJP spokesperson Vaishnavi Gaur said the delegation would place the same demands it has been raising since the protests began."We will be putting forward our demands, which we have been consistent with from the first day," she said.According to Gaur, the key demands include the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan, compensation for the families affected by the NEET controversy, and withdrawal of all FIRs registered against what she described as "innocent protesters."Following Wangchuk's decision to end his fast, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke thanked him for what he called an extraordinary act of courage."We are relieved and grateful that Sonam sir has ended his hunger strike after 26 days. Thank you for your extraordinary courage and sacrifice. By putting your own life on the line, you awakened the conscience of an entire nation. Your life is far too precious to this country," Dipke wrote in a post on X.Despite Wangchuk ending his fast, the CJP has maintained that its peaceful protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar will continue until its demands, including Pradhan's resignation, are addressed.
Article Summary: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) delegation will meet Union ministers at the Constitution Club of India at 12.30 pm on Friday. Meeting comes a day after activist Sonam Wangchuk ended his 26-day hunger strike at Medanta Hospital.

Article Title: SC: Will go the extra mile to fix issues, make NEET foolproof
Article Text:
SC assures Neet will be foolproof

NEW DELHI: Amid street protests by the youth against paper leaks and demands that govt fix accountability and bring reforms, the Supreme Court Friday said the system's ad hocism was "troubling", which could not be allowed to go on and assured that it would "tread an extra mile" to fix the problems and make NEET foolproof.With solicitor general Tushar Mehta contending that govt was ready to tread "10 extra miles" to protect the interests of students and that the matter was being supervised at the highest level, a bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe asked him to expeditiously take a decision. It granted time till Aug 3 to brief them about the contours of the new system.The court also sought the Centre's response on implementing computer-based test for medical entrance on the lines of IIT-JEE.The court was hearing a batch of petitions, including ones filed by the Federation of All India Medical Association and United Doctors Front, seeking the court's intervention to make NEET tamper-free. The SG, at the outset of the hearing, said the issue was under serious consideration of govt and sought adjournment for a few days. He said some developments were likely to take place soon.The bench, however, pointed out various issues which govt needed to address, including implementation of recommendations of the high-level committee headed by former Isro chairman K Radhakrishnan."We will highlight a couple of things we wanted to indicate... Last time, you mentioned the Radhakrishnan committee's recommendations. There is a specific reference to the governing board. So your affidavit should indicate what has been done with respect to the governing board, which would consist of transparency, nominations and stakeholders," the bench said.SC said it will keep monitoring the process till the system is institutionalised. "We are focusing on institutionalisation. Ad-hocism has troubled us the most throughout these years.""A very important aspect is the transition to computer-based testing.... Can it be shifted? How will the data be transferred? How will the data be protected? Data safety is the most important aspect. You indicate to us. Cybersecurity, who is to undertake it, how it is to be conducted etc," the bench asked.Dr Radhakrishnan, head of the monitoring committee constituted by SC in 2024 to suggest ways to strengthen NEET, earlier informed the court the committee had submitted 35 long-term recommendations and around 60 short-term recommendations, most of which had already been implemented. He said the reforms had largely yielded positive results in NEET-PG 2025, which was conducted "mostly satisfactorily" except for some issues such as power outages.
Article Summary: Supreme Court says system's ad hocism was "troubling", which could not be allowed to go on. Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe granted time till Aug 3 to brief them about the contours of the new system.

Article Title: 20-year-old US student, army officer's son, dies as car plunges into open drain in south Delhi
Article Text:
The circumstances that led to the crash are being probed, say police





NEW DELHI: A 20-year-old student home from US was killed when the car he was driving overturned and plunged into an open drain in south Delhi's Vasant Kunj early Friday.A young woman travelling with him escaped from the vehicle and survived.The victim was identified as Yashvendra, who recently returned to India and was staying with a friend in Delhi Cantonment area. His father is an Army officer posted in Kolkata.The accident took place around 6am near the Nangal Dewat drain. Police teams pulled the vehicle out of the drain and dragged out Yashvendra. He was taken to a hospital, where doctors declared him brought dead.Police said because of rain the road where the car crashed was slushy.It might have caused the car to skid, hit a tree, overturn and fall into the drain, they said.The girl, in a statement to police, too, blamed the slippery road for the accident.The drain had no cover or retaining wall to prevent vehicles or pedestrians from falling into it.“Yashvendra was accompanied by his friend, a woman, who is also studying in the same business school as him in the US. They were coming towards Mahipalpur from a friend’s house in Vasant Kunj Enclave.It is suspected that he lost control of the vehicle when he took a sharp turn,” a senior police officer said.The vehicle belongs to the woman, but Yashvendra was driving. The woman was able to get out of the car as she was able to open the door on her side after the car fell in the drain. The officer said the man, however, was stuck inside and the roof of the vehicle also completely collapsed. The woman suffered minor injuries.A case has not been registered yet, police said.The circumstances that led to the crash, including the speed of the vehicle and whether any other factor contributed to the accident, are being probed. CCTV footage from the area is also being examined.
Article Summary: A 20-year-old student home from US was killed when the car he was driving overturned and plunged into an open drain in south Delhi's Vasant Kunj early Friday. A young woman travelling with him escaped from the vehicle and survived. The circumstances that led to the crash are being probed, say police.

Article Title: Florida scientists used female Burmese pythons as live lures to find invasive males in the Everglades, but 3 million camera-trap photos produced only four python detections
Article Text:
Conservancy biologists with a 16ft, 135lb female Burmese python found while radio-tracking a male scout snake in southwest Florida in February 2025.

Southeastern Naturalist

Captivity stress and chemical signals

The ongoing battle in the Everglades

Removal programs and public support

Florida scientists used female Burmese pythons as live lures to find invasive males in the Everglades, but 3 million camera-trap photos produced only four python detections.A study published in the journalshows that placing wild-caught female Burmese pythons (Python bivittatus) in cages across the Greater Everglades Ecosystem failed to draw in wild males.Over a 90-day field test at 12 locations, researchers filtered more than three million camera-trap photos using artificial intelligence software. They recorded just three python visits at the cages holding female lures and one visit at empty control cages.The study, titled "Not so fatal attraction: Captive female Burmese Python lures do not improve wild python detection," was written by Alex D. Potash, Maggie Jones, Michael Kirkland, Jenna Cole, Kristen Hart, and Robert A. McCleery. The research record was published by the USGS Publications Warehouse and carried out through the USGS Wetland and Aquatic Research Center.In controlled laboratory settings, male pythons show a strong interest in the scents given off by breeding females. However, the scientists suggest that the stress of living in cages may have stopped the captive females from releasing pheromones, removing the chemical scent needed to attract wild males.Understanding how pythons communicate is still limited. The authors note that finding better care methods to reduce stress in captured females could improve future tests, while further work on python chemistry might help create fake scents to track the invasive snakes.The failed female lure test follows another setback with scent tracking. In an August 2025 study published in Management of Biological Invasions, titled "Mammalian scent lures fail to increase detections of invasive Burmese pythons (Python bivittatus)," researchers tested whether rabbit scent could replace live prey.Written by Storm Miller, Michael Kirkland, Kristen Hart, and Robert A. McCleery of the USGS Wetland and Aquatic Research Center, the 84-day experiment across 21 sites brought only 11 python sightings. Four pythons were seen near rabbit scent lures (poop, urine, and hair) and seven near plain soil. While the rabbit scent attracted more native snakes by drawing in live mice and rats, it did not draw in pythons.These scent experiments show how hard it is to find a top predator that has wiped out native mammals like marsh rabbits, foxes, raccoons, and deer.Pythons spread through South Florida in the 1990s when escaped or released pets entered the wild. Today, tens of thousands live in the wetlands. Females can lay up to 100 eggs a year, making control efforts urgent.Despite scent lure challenges, state teams and conservation groups report steady progress through hunting and radio tracking.The Conservancy of Southwest Florida recently announced it has removed 20 tons of pythons from the wild over a decade, setting a single-season record by taking 6,300 pounds of snakes out of a 200-square-mile area since November.The conservancy's main strategy relies on fitting wild male "scout" snakes with radio trackers during the November-to-April breeding season. The tagged males lead biologists straight to breeding groups, allowing teams to catch large females before they lay eggs.“There’s very good evidence that the scout snake program is our most effective and least biased method. It doesn’t just limit us to targeting human accessible areas and it’s super targeted toward those reproductive females,” said Andrew Durso, a herpetologist at Florida Gulf Coast University. “But it’s expensive to radio-track these males into remote parts of the Everglades where you can’t go very easily. You need air support from a helicopter, which ups the price per python removed. It’s all a balance sheet of how do we want to spend money?”Ian Bartoszek, science project manager and chief wildlife scientist at the Conservancy of Southwest Florida, noted that his team's work has stopped roughly 20,000 eggs from hatching since 2013.“Through years of research we’ve developed science-based methods to track this apex predator more effectively and mitigate its damage to our native wildlife population,” said Bartoszek. “Burmese pythons are impressive creatures that are here from no fault of their own. As wildlife biologists, we have tremendous respect for all snake species. However, we understand the impact invasive pythons are having on the biodiversity in our area and we humanely remove them from the ecosystem. ”The South Florida Water Management District has separately tracked and removed over 15,650 pythons through its Python Elimination Program, which hires paid snake hunters. Public support stays high, aided by annual events like the Florida Python Challenge, which drew 895 hunters who caught 195 pythons in 2024.Mike Kirkland, python program manager at the district, sees signs that removal work is helping key areas.“Every single python that’s removed is positive for the environment,” said Kirkland. “We’re getting better and better at removing this invasive species. We’re learning more about their behavior and life history, and their non-native range here in south Florida, which is leading to more removals and hopefully innovation and novel strategies going forward.”Kirkland added that removing every single python across the wetlands may not be possible, but local populations are changing.“Progress is being made. Anecdotally we’re seeing some demographic shifts, and regionally, we’re seeing less larger size-class pythons in certain areas. That’s a direct result of our management efforts, and our partners’ management efforts,” Kirkland said.“As with most environmental issues, a multi-pronged strategy of different efforts working in concert with one another is really the best path forward,” Kirkland added. “In the future I see the python population being greatly reduced, and to a point where we can begin to see a robust return of our native animal populations, which is why we’re doing all this to begin with. I’m confident we’re going to be able to manage this species to the point where we’re seeing our deer populations, our foxes, our possums, our raccoons and so on, restored to the Everglades. ”Burmese pythons (Python bivittatus) are among the world's largest snakes, commonly growing 10–16 feet (3–5 metres) long, with some exceeding 18 feet (5.5 metres). Native to Southeast Asia, they are non-venomous constrictors that kill prey by cutting off blood flow before swallowing it whole using flexible jaws. They can eat animals as large as deer and alligators, then survive for weeks or even months without another meal. Females may lay more than 100 eggs in one clutch and protect them until they hatch. In Florida's Everglades, where they are invasive, Burmese pythons have caused major declines in several native mammal populations.
Article Summary: Florida scientists used female Burmese pythons as live lures to find invasive males in the Everglades, but 3 million camera-trap photos produced only four python detections. The stress of living in cages may have stopped the captive females from releasing pheromones, removing the chemical scent needed to attract wild males.

Article Title: In the 1980s, Scotland planted commercial trees across parts of a 9,000-year-old peatland; decades later, conservationists are removing them to protect wildlife and keep its stored carbon in the groun
Article Text:
A Common Greenshank stood on the edge of a pool of water.

Destruction of a wild habitat

A Common Greenshank stood on the edge of a pool of water.

Reversing the damage at Forsinard Flows

Government backing and broader targets

Bringing communities into the bog

In the 1980s, Scotland planted commercial trees across parts of a 9,000-year-old peatland; decades later, conservationists are removing them to protect wildlife and keep its stored carbon in the ground.The massive project centers on the Flow Country, a vast area of wet bog covering over 400,000 hectares across Caithness and Sutherland in northern Scotland. In July 2024, UNESCO named the area a World Heritage Site, placing it alongside natural treasures like the Great Barrier Reef and the Grand Canyon. It became the world's first peatland to get this special status. King Charles III marked the event by visiting the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) Forsinard Flows reserve to reveal a special plaque.Despite its global fame today, large parts of this ancient landscape were nearly ruined forty years ago. During the 1980s, tax rules and government grants encouraged forestry companies to drain the wet ground, build deer fences, put in roads, and plant long rows of commercial trees.The quick growth of these tree farms hurt the delicate bog. The trees pulled water out of the muddy ground, causing the deep peat soil to dry out and break down.This loss of open land threatened local birds that need wide, treeless spaces to build their nests. Before government action stopped the planting, the region lost about 900 pairs of Golden Plovers, nearly 800 pairs of Dunlins, and 130 pairs of Greenshanks. The area is also a vital home for Hen Harriers, insect-eating sundew plants, Common Scoters, and Red-throated Divers, which lay eggs near small bog pools.Pressure from the Nature Conservancy Council, the RSPB, and other green groups eventually forced the government to change its plans. In January 1988, Malcolm Rifkind, who was then Secretary of State for Scotland, announced that the government would protect over 140,000 hectares of peatland as Sites of Special Scientific Interest. Later that year, Nigel Lawson, then Chancellor, ended the tax breaks and grants that made tree planting on peat profitable.Real cleanup work started in 1994 when the RSPB bought the Forsinard Estate in the middle of the Flow Country, paid for by donations from its members. Today, RSPB Forsinard Flows is the largest nature reserve managed by the charity in the UK.Using money from two big European Union LIFE Nature grants, conservation teams tested ways to cut down the commercial trees, block drainage ditches, and soak the ground again. The main goal is to turn thousands of cleared hectares back into healthy, working bogs.The choice to cut down trees goes beyond helping wildlife. Peatlands are often called the lungs of the Earth because they absorb and trap carbon. The Flow Country alone holds roughly 400 million tonnes of carbon in its soil, which is more carbon than all of the UK’s forests and woods combined. When peat dries out, that trapped carbon leaks back into the air as heat-trapping gas.Peatlands cover over two million hectares across Scotland, making up 25 per cent of the country's land area and more than 60 per cent of all UK peatlands.To help fix this land, the Scottish Government promised £250 million over ten years to restore 250,000 hectares of damaged peatlands by 2030 through its Peatland ACTION Programme. Official records show that over 75,000 hectares have been fixed so far, including a record 10,360 hectares completed during the 2023-24 financial year.Scotland's peatland policy focuses on three main steps: protecting healthy sites, taking care of working land, and fixing damaged areas. New science shows that other practical steps, like keeping farm animals and deer from overgrazing, re-wetting farm soil, and changing how grassy peatlands are used, can cut gas emissions even further.Fixing remote peatlands means working in tough conditions, where cold weather and wet mud make field tasks hard. To gain public and political support, conservation groups built better visitor spots at Forsinard Flows.The reserve now has a lookout tower that offers visitors panoramic views of the surrounding landscape. Recent investments have also added modern research facilities and on-site accommodation, allowing scientists, researchers and volunteers to stay at the reserve while studying how healthy bogs store carbon and support the return of rare bird species.Beside storing carbon and creating homes for wildlife, the Scottish Government sees peatland repair as a way to create green jobs. The long cleanup effort is bringing countryside work to northern Scotland, helping local hotels and cafes, and building up green tourism.
Article Summary: Peatlands cover over two million hectares across Scotland, making up 25 per cent of the country's land area. The Flow Country alone holds roughly 400 million tonnes of carbon in its soil, which is more carbon than all of the UK’s forests and woods combined. When peat dries out, that trapped carbon leaks back into the air as heat-trapping gas.

Article Title: Vietnam moves to bar under-16s from posting, commenting on social media
Article Text:
Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the idea of requiring social media accounts for children under 16 to be registered through a parent or guardian? Yes, it enhances safety No, it restricts freedom 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Vietnam is planning to require social media platforms to stop users under the age of 16 from posting content, commenting or reacting to posts, under a draft decree aimed at strengthening online protections for children, according to a document reviewed by Reuters.The proposed rules would require social media accounts belonging to children under 16 to be registered using the information of a parent or legal guardian, who would be responsible for supervising the content viewed by children and the amount of time they spend on the platforms.The draft decree also requires social media companies to use technical measures to identify child users and ensure that they receive age-appropriate content. Platforms would have to provide the highest level of privacy protection for child accounts and proactively detect, warn and block access to content related to violence, pornography, gambling, drugs, suicide and other harmful material."The primary objective is not to ban or excessively restrict children's access to social media, but rather to ensure that when children use social media services, they are placed in an age-appropriate environment and protected from inappropriate risks," deputy culture minister Phan Tam said on Thursday during a meeting to discuss the proposed rules.The proposal comes as governments across the world tighten regulations on children's use of social media amid growing concerns over online safety and the impact of harmful content on young users' mental health.Earlier this week, French lawmakers approved a ban on social media access for children under 15. Australia became the first country to impose such a ban, while several other countries are considering similar measures.The draft decree also proposes new restrictions on online gaming by minors. Game operators would be required to verify users' ages, register accounts of children under 16 through a parent or legal guardian, and limit users under 16 to a maximum of 60 minutes of gameplay per day across games offered by the same company.The draft decree has not yet been finalised and may be revised before it is formally adopted.
Article Summary: Vietnam is planning to require social media platforms to stop users under the age of 16 from posting content, commenting or reacting to posts. The draft decree is aimed at strengthening online protections for children. The proposal comes as governments across the world tighten regulations on children's use of social media.

Article Title: Inside Tuvalu: This tiny island nation has just one airline, almost no tourists, and a future threatened by rising seas
Article Text:
Why Tuvalu is considered one of the most vulnerable nations on earth

What NASA's analysis actually found

A rising tide already visible on the ground

Daily life on a shrinking runway between the ocean

A cash economy that only recently modernised

Why a nation this small carries such outsized stakes

Tuvalu is one of the least visited countries on earth. A single airline, Fiji Airways, operates the only scheduled flights in and out, connecting the capital atoll of Funafuti to Fiji a few times a week, and there is no other way to reach the country by air. The entire nation is made up of nine coral atolls covering roughly 26 square kilometres, smaller than many major airports, and is home to just under 11,000 people. Life here has always moved differently from most of the world, shaped by close communal ties and a cash-based economy that only recently saw its first ATMs installed. But scientists now warn Tuvalu faces a far bigger question than isolation: whether the country will remain habitable at all as sea levels continue to rise. Tuvalu's government has also explored more unconventional responses to this crisis, including efforts to digitally preserve the nation's culture and even legal identity, in case rising seas eventually force its population to relocate entirely.Tuvalu's islands sit at an average elevation of only about two metres above sea level, among the lowest of any country on the planet. According to a technical report titled Assessment of Sea Level Rise and Associated Impacts for Tuvalu , produced by NASA 's Sea Level Change Team in support of the United Nations-backed Rising Nations Initiative, Tuvalu has already begun experiencing measurable impacts from the combined effects of rising oceans, storms and natural ocean variability, effects the report expects to worsen in the years ahead.According to NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory , Pacific island nations including Tuvalu, Kiribati and Fiji will experience at least 15 centimetres of sea level rise over the next 30 years, a figure the agency describes as effectively locked in regardless of whether global greenhouse gas emissions change going forward. The analysis was carried out by researchers at the University of Hawaii, working alongside scientists from the University of Colorado and Virginia Tech, at the request of Pacific island governments themselves, and in coordination with the United States Department of State. Nadya Vinogradova Shiffer, who directs ocean physics programs within NASA's Earth Science Division, noted that sea levels will continue rising for centuries, bringing more frequent flooding to coastal communities across the region regardless of near-term emissions decisions.Grace Malie, a youth leader from Tuvalu involved with the Rising Nations Initiative, told NASA that accurate science and data can help her community understand exactly what these sea level projections mean in practice, adding that this information also supports early warning systems the country is actively developing. Malie described the stakes bluntly, saying the future of Tuvalu's young people is already at stake, and that climate change represents a matter of justice and survival rather than simply an environmental concern. NASA researchers noted a genuine shortage of on-the-ground measurement data in Pacific nations like Tuvalu, which is part of why the agency has begun combining satellite-based sea level data with ground station measurements and more detailed land elevation mapping specifically for these vulnerable coastlines.Despite the scale of the threat it faces, Tuvalu remains almost entirely disconnected from global tourism. Fiji Airways is the sole carrier serving the country, and flights operate only a few times each week between Funafuti and Fiji, making Tuvalu one of the hardest countries in the world to simply visit. Funafuti International Airport itself is modest by international standards, a single terminal building sitting so close to the surrounding village that locals can walk directly onto the runway whenever no flight is scheduled.Until quite recently, every transaction in Tuvalu, by locals and visitors alike, had to be conducted entirely in cash, since the country had no ATMs anywhere on its islands. That changed in April 2025, when the National Bank of Tuvalu, the country's only bank, installed the nation's first five ATMs on Funafuti, including machines at Vaiaku village and the airport itself. Prime Minister Feleti Teo described the moment as a significant milestone for the country, while the bank's general manager, Siose Teo, called it a transformative switch that would open doors to broader economic participation for Tuvaluans. Even with this change, banking infrastructure across the country remains extremely limited compared to almost anywhere else in the world.Whatever infrastructure changes come next, the core threat facing Tuvalu remains the same one NASA's sea level science team has been documenting for years: a slow, largely irreversible rise in sea level that threatens not just periodic flooding but the long-term habitability of the country itself. With no natural elevation to retreat to and limited land available for adaptation, Tuvalu has become one of the clearest real-world test cases for what rising seas mean for entire nations, not just coastlines, making its quiet, rarely visited atolls a subject of growing scientific and diplomatic attention far beyond their tiny population and remote location in the middle of the Pacific.
Article Summary: Tuvalu's islands sit at an average elevation of only about two metres above sea level, among the lowest of any country on the planet. Pacific island nations including Tuvalu, Kiribati and Fiji will experience at least 15 centimetres of sea level rise over the next 30 years.

Article Title: Iran war risk: JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warns of oil shocks, sticky inflation and higher interest rates
Article Text: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has warned that the ongoing war in Iran could trigger oil and commodity price shocks, keeping inflation elevated and pushing interest rates higher than current market expectations, Reuters reported.The warning came in his annual letter to shareholders, a day after US President Donald Trump escalated pressure on Iran by threatening to target key infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz is not reopened."Now, because of the war in Iran, we additionally face the potential for significant ongoing oil and commodity price shocks, along with the reshaping of global supply chains, which may lead to stickier inflation and ultimately higher interest rates than markets currently expect," Dimon said, news agency Reuters quoted as saying.Dimon, who has led JPMorgan for two decades, also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China."The challenges we all face are significant," he added.He said it remains uncertain whether the Iran war will achieve US objectives, while warning that nuclear proliferation remains the biggest risk linked to Iran.Markets have already begun pricing in these risks, with expectations of interest rate cuts this year largely fading amid rising inflation concerns triggered by the conflict.Last week, the benchmark S&P 500 index recorded its worst quarterly performance since 2022, weighed down by rising energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty since late February.Dimon noted that the US economy remains resilient, with consumers continuing to earn and spend, and businesses staying broadly healthy, though signs of weakening have emerged.He cautioned that economic strength has been supported by significant government deficit spending and past stimulus, while infrastructure investment needs continue to grow.At the same time, he pointed to positives such as fiscal stimulus under President Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill", deregulation policies and rising capital expenditure driven by artificial intelligence.On financial stability, Dimon said the $1.8-trillion private credit market "probably" does not pose a systemic risk, despite investor concerns and recent withdrawals from such funds.However, he warned that in a downturn, losses across leveraged lending could exceed expectations as credit standards have weakened.Private credit markets also lack transparency and rigorous valuation benchmarks, increasing the risk of investor exits if conditions worsen, he said.Separately, Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical" and "very flawed".He said JPMorgan’s GSIB surcharge would fall only to 5.0%, a level he described as “absurd” and “un-American”, arguing it penalises the bank’s scale and performance.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warns Iran war could trigger oil and commodity price shocks. He also highlighted broader geopolitical risks, including the war in Ukraine, tensions in the Middle East and friction with China. Dimon criticised revised US capital rules, including Basel III and GSIB surcharge norms, calling aspects of the proposals "nonsensical"

Article Title: How selling Alaska in 1867 was a costly mistake for Russia
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

Why Russia agreed to the Alaska purchase

The hidden wealth Russia gave away

Strategic and geopolitical consequences







In 1867, Russia’s decision to sell Alaska to America turned out to be a historic mistake that was to go unnoticed for years to come. The sum paid by the US was only $7,200,000. Although, in the light of the circumstances at the time, it appeared logical, retrospectively, the act looks extremely shortsighted. Russia found itself economically constrained, geographically far away from the region and fearful of its falling into the hands of the British without any compensation. In reality, however, the region had proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Its vast reserves of oil, gold, and natural resources would later transform it into one of the most economically significant territories in the United States.The choice of selling Alaska was based on economic and political reasons. By the middle of the 19th century, the Russian Empire experienced financial difficulties as a result of the expensive Crimean War. It had become increasingly hard for the country to manage such remote and thinly populated areas as Alaska.According to EBSCO , “the Russian-American Company was in decline, and the colony failed to yield any profit”.In addition to this, the lucrative fur trade had declined, making the territory much less economically valuable for the empire.At the same time, Russia was afraid that Britain might capture Alaska in case another war broke out between the two countries. Selling the colony to the friendly United States appeared as a logical step. As the Office of the Historian states, William H. Seward, U.S. Secretary of State, “it was a chance to expand its influence in North America and hinder further growth of Britain”.For Russia, the transaction was a chance to minimise the losses. However, it greatly undervalued the potential of Alaska.Another thing that Russia did not expect was the amount of riches that Alaska possessed. Within several decades after the acquisition, the state saw discoveries of enormous deposits of gold, oil, and other minerals.“Alaska has produced more than 40 million ounces of gold,” according to the US Geological Survey. Furthermore, Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) . But even more importantly, the state's oil deposits turned out to be extremely valuable. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968 and became one of North America's biggest.In retrospect, the amount paid by the Americans, $7.2 million, or two cents per acre, was rather laughable. According to Howard I. Kushner , the deal “robbed Russia of an enormously rich territory, the true value of which would only be recognised in the twentieth century.”In addition to resources, there is the question of strategy and how important Alaska is to the United States from a strategic standpoint. This is a very good place when it comes to defence strategy. It borders on the Arctic Ocean and also happens to be close to Russia.During the period of the Cold War, the Alaskan region became a frontier area for the United States, becoming home to military facilities and warning systems.According to Col. Michael J. Forsyth, U.S. Army, the closeness of Russia and Alaska, only about ninety kilometres apart across the Bering Strait, meant that this region became highly significant to the United States' defence plans.From today's point of view, the strategic location of Alaska makes the state very important to the policies of the U.S. related to the Arctic, energy security, and even environmental policies.Thinking back, what seems clear to us now is that the Russians sold Alaska due to immediate needs rather than future considerations. In order to solve the problem, they lost a valuable resource for Russia.Conclusively, the Alaska Purchase should not have been done as it has had a significant impact that will remain throughout history.
Article Summary: Russia sold Alaska to the U.S. in 1867 for only $7,200,000. The sale was based on economic and political reasons. However, the region proved immensely valuable both strategically and naturally. Alaska is home to some of the world's most significant undeveloped mineral deposits. The Prudhoe Bay oil field was discovered in 1968.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies





AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: What a paan seller's life reveals about resilience and women's agency
Article Text:
Determined to turn his life around, Birbal Chaurasiya opened a paan stall and devoted himself to hard work





NEW DELHI: If you stand on the steps of the Express Building on Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg, you will notice two open-air stalls selling paan, cigarettes and cold drinks.Birbal Chaurasiya's makeshift kiosk has stood on the right since the days when only a handful of cars used to be parked in the lane.The automobiles were almost like their owners' calling cards: newspaper baron Ramnath Goenka's black Fiat and editor S Mulgaonkar's white Ambassador.As a teenager, Birbal had escaped a troubled home by taking the Kashi Vishwanath Express from Pratapgarh in east UP in the early 1970s.He was carrying Rs 175, money he owed someone and would return with apologies decades later.A village friend who accompanied him disappeared once the money was over.Birbal would wash dishes, serve tea in a dhaba behind The Times of India building.At night he would sleep in the cycle stand, curling up like a prawn over flattened cardboard boxes, using the famous Nepa newsprint as a make-shift blanket in winter.Early morning ragpickers would strip him of the cover.Chaurasiyas are traditionally associated with selling 'paan' (betel) leaves.Birbal switched to the familiar profession after finding out that fellow villagers were doing the same at Chandni Chowk and earning more.A wicker-basket would become his portable stall. He would tour Daryaganj, Kaudiya Pul, even the pleasure centres of GB Road, where a senior madame became his regular customer."I trudged about 30-35 kms every day," recalls Birbal, now in his mid-sixties.One night while he was sleeping, someone filched Rs 70 that he had saved over months.The setback pushed him to share a rented room at Kotla.The generous Express Canteen owner would offer a 50% discount, making him pay 50 paise instead of Re 1 for the 'thali.'An indulgent doorman would let him watch plays like 'Romeo and Juliet' at Mandi House.The tide turned with time. Birbal's income rose dramatically once he set up the roofless stall in 1980.He would now occasionally gorge on butter chicken at the Peshawari hotel in Daryaganj and pay bills back home. In 1985, he bought a plot of land in Vaishali, Ghaziabad. "Few had the foresight to do it then," he says.It's drizzling. Dressed in a faded pink kurta and pyjamas, Birbal sits cross-legged at the kiosk.A thick tarpaulin sheet shelters the stall. He multi-tasks with seamless abandon, talking on the mobile about pending orders, handing out cash to a dealer and preparing paan for a customer.Some customers just pick up a cigarette, light it and walk away without paying or talking.Birbal scribbles down something in a register. "They always pay," he smiles with the understanding of Lallan Mian of 'Chashme Buddoor'.Birbal also serves 'beetroot kanji', 'aam panna', 'nimbu paani'.The business diversification was prompted by a devastating fire that swept through the third and fourth floors of Express Building in 1996.As several companies temporarily relocated, sales dramatically dropped. "I was depressed," he says.Those were tough years. In 2000, his elder daughter, Geeta, cleared the entry-level CA Foundation.His ideas on women's education were partly shaped by his interaction with journalists who often came to his shop for paan or cigarettes."Some were women reporters; all intelligent, articulate and confident. I understood that progress is linked to education. Which is why I decided to educate my daughters," he says.Serendipity arrived one summer afternoon. Birbal shared some homemade 'bel (wood apple) ka sherbet' with a small group of friends and acquaintances.They were effusive. Some offered to be regular customers."The next day I made Rs 160 after selling two bottles. My total daily sales from the paan shop was just Rs 150 those days," he remembers.Birbal had stumbled upon a way out of the fiscal mess. Over the next few years, with his wife's culinary support, he would also serve pickles, murabba and a variety of homemade drinks.Slowly as the companies returned to the building, so did the customers.Years later, his mobile phone rang one afternoon. "You have become the father of a chartered accountant," his son said on the phone. Birbal took a while before he realised that he was talking about his elder sister."That moment I realised my life had not been wasted," he says with undisguised emotion.Despite MCD's occasional disruption that forces vendors like him to shut shop, Birbal is mentally relaxed nowadays.His younger daughter Pooja is a cost accountant and son Umesh an insurance agent. He goes on family holidays to places like Manali.And he speaks with quiet pride about flying his mom to Varanasi. He still opens around 9 am and packs up only around 10.30 at night."But I don't do it for money anymore. I love the routine, my work," he says.Over the decades Birbal has seen the service lane mutate into an overcrowded area clogged with cars and people. Journalists have morphed too."The earlier generation would talk about literature. That doesn't happen anymore," he says, "But some young reporters still have the fire. That's what I like."Delhi is often cold and hard,or both, towards the deprived but the city also holds out a sliver of promise that the hardiest and the persistent cling on to.Birbal isn't the kind of achiever celebrated on the TED stage, but his life speaks to thousands of migrants who arrive every day in the unsparing capital hoping to survive, and maybe, carve out a better life.
Article Summary: Birbal Chaurasiya is a chaurasiyas, traditionally associated with selling 'paan' (betel) leaves. As a teenager, he escaped a troubled home by taking the Kashi Vishwanath Express from Pratapgarh in east UP. Determined to turn his life around, Birbal opened a paan stall and devoted himself to hard work.

Article Title: Mega Block on Central Railway main and Trans-Harbour Line today; suburban services to be affected
Article Text:
No daytime block is scheduled on the Western Railway suburban section today. (Representative Image)





MUMBAI: Central Railway's Mumbai Division will operate a mega block on the Main Line between Thane and Kalyan and on the Trans-Harbour Line between Thane and Vashi/Nerul today to undertake essential engineering and maintenance works aimed at ensuring the safety and reliability of railway infrastructure.No daytime block is scheduled on the Western Railway suburban section today.On the Main Line, the block will be in force on the Up and Down Fast Lines between Thane and Kalyan from 10.40 am to 3.40 pm.During this period, fast and semi-fast suburban services will be diverted to slow lines, with additional halts at Kalva, Mumbra and Diva stations.These trains are expected to reach their destinations approximately 10 minutes behind schedule. Several Mail and Express trains will also be diverted via the 5th and 6th lines between Thane and Kalyan.On the Trans-Harbour Line, services between Thane and Vashi/Nerul will remain suspended from 11.10 am to 4.10 pm. Several services operating between Thane, Vashi, Nerul and Panvel during the block period will remain cancelled.

The block will be in force on the Up and Down Fast Lines from 10.40 am to 3.40 pm. No daytime block is scheduled on the Western Railway suburban section.
